chapterNote: The famous poem of the times (vv. 1-8) is not a shrug at fate; it is a catalogue of appointments. Fourteen paired opposites, twenty-eight 'times' in all, span birth to death, war to peace — and every one of them is fixed from above while man is carried through them from below. The Preacher then names the ache this creates: God has planted olam, eternity, in the human heart, so that a creature made for forever must live inside seasons it cannot see past (v. 11). The chapter's comforts are sturdy ones: God's work stands permanent so that men will fear Him, He will bring every deed to judgment in its own appointed time, and meanwhile the gift remains — eat, drink, rejoice in your work. But the chapter refuses false comfort too: seen strictly from under the sun, man and beast draw the same breath and go to the same dust, and only God knows the difference in their endings.

1.text: For everything there is an appointed season, and a time for every matter and every delight under heaven:
1.amp: To every thing there is a season [an appointed hour], and a time [et] to every purpose [chephets — matter, delight, desire] under the heaven [shamayim]:
1.notes: The word for 'season' (H2165) is zeman, a fixed appointment, and et (H6256) is the fitting time. chephets (H2656) usually means delight or desire; even the purposes here are things men set their hearts on, all of them scheduled from above.

2.text: A time for bearing and a time for dying; a time for planting, and a time for uprooting what was planted;
2.amp: A time [et] to be born [yalad — literally 'to bear'] and a time to die; a time to plant [nata], and a time to pluck up [uproot] that which is planted;
2.notes: yalad (H3205) is active, 'to bear' (so the KJV margin): the mother's hour, not the child's choosing, which is the point — no one schedules his own birth. nata (H5193), to plant and fix, is the same verb as the king's vineyards in chapter 2.

3.text: A time for killing and a time for healing; a time for breaking down, and a time for building up;
3.amp: A time [et] to kill [harag] and a time to heal [rapha — cure, repair]; a time to break down [parats — breach, burst through] and a time to build [banah];
3.notes: harag (H2026) is the word for slaying in war and judgment, and rapha (H7495) the word for God's own healing (cf. Exodus 15:26). parats (H6555) is to breach a wall; banah (H1129) to raise one: history swings between demolition and construction.

4.text: A time for weeping and a time for laughing; a time for mourning, and a time for dancing;
4.amp: A time [et] to weep [bakah — weep bitterly] and a time to laugh [sachaq]; a time to mourn [saphad — wail, lament aloud] and a time to dance;
4.notes: saphad (H5594) is the loud, public wailing of a funeral procession, and the dance-word (H7540, raqad) is its exact opposite, the leaping of festival joy. Both get their hour; neither is permanent.

5.text: A time for throwing stones away and a time for gathering stones in; a time for embracing, and a time for keeping far from every embrace;
5.amp: A time [et] to cast away [shalak — throw, fling] stones [even] and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace [chabaq] and a time to be far [rachaq] from embracing;
5.notes: Scattering stones ruined a field and gathering them cleared one for use (cf. 2 Kings 3:19, 25; Isaiah 5:2): the pair covers both war-work and farm-work. chabaq (H2263) is the embrace of affection, and rachaq (H7368), to keep far off, is the Hebrew behind the KJV's 'refrain'.

6.text: A time for seeking and a time for counting as lost; a time for keeping, and a time for casting away;
6.amp: A time [et] to seek [baqash — search for] and a time to lose [abad — let perish, give up as gone]; a time to keep [shamar — guard, preserve] and a time to cast away [shalak];
6.notes: abad (H6) is to perish or be lost: there is an hour when the wise man stops searching and writes the loss down. shamar (H8104), to guard and keep, is the treasuring instinct, and it too has a closing time.

7.text: A time for tearing and a time for sewing; a time for keeping silent, and a time for speaking out;
7.amp: A time [et] to rend [tear the garment] and a time to sew; a time to keep silence [chashah — be still, hold one's peace] and a time to speak [dabar];
7.notes: Tearing the garment was the gesture of grief (cf. Job 1:20), and sewing it up marked mourning's end. chashah (H2814) is deliberate stillness, the discipline of the shut mouth; dabar (H1696) its equally disciplined opposite.

8.text: A time for loving and a time for hating; a time of war, and a time of peace.
8.amp: A time [et] to love [ahab — love, delight in] and a time to hate [sane]; a time of war [milchamah] and a time of peace [shalom — peace, wholeness, welfare].
8.notes: ahab (H157) and sane (H8130) are the poem's last personal pair; milchamah (H4421) and shalom (H7965) its last public one. The catalogue ends on shalom, wholeness — the note the whole list leans toward.

9.text: What lasting profit, then, does the worker get from all the toil he labors at?
9.amp: What profit [yithron — surplus, what is left over] has he that works [asah] in that wherein he labours [amel]?
9.notes: The bookkeeping question of 1:3 returns, aimed now at the poem: yithron (H3504), the surplus. If every hour is appointed from above, what does the man inside the hours actually add? amel (H6001) is the toiler himself.

10.text: I have seen the task that God has given the sons of man to be humbled and exercised by.
10.amp: I have seen [raah] the travail [inyan — task, business], which God [Elohim] has given [natan] to the sons of men [adam] to be exercised [anah — humbled, afflicted] in it.
10.notes: inyan (H6045), the task or business unique to this book, and anah (H6031), to humble: the burden is real, but the verse quietly names its source and purpose. God gave it, and it is doing its work on us.

11.text: He has made everything beautiful in its own time. He has also planted eternity in their heart, yet in such a way that man cannot search out the work God has done from the beginning all the way to the end.
11.amp: He has made [asah] every thing beautiful [yapheh — fitting, lovely] in its time [et]: also He has set [natan] eternity [olam — the world, the long horizon of forever] in their heart [leb], so that no [beli] man [adam] can find out [matsa] the work [maaseh] that God [Elohim] makes from the beginning [rosh] to the end.
11.notes: The pivot of the chapter. yapheh (H3303) is 'beautiful' in the sense of fitting and right, each thing lovely in its appointed et (H6256). olam (H5769), eternity, is planted in the leb (H3820): man carries a forever-shaped ache through a world of seasons, able to sense the whole story yet never to matsa (H4672), find out, its span.

12.text: I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice, and to do good, as long as life lasts.
12.amp: I know [yada] that there is no good [tov] in them, but for a man to rejoice [samach], and to do [asah] good [tov] in his life [chay]:
12.notes: samach (H8055), to rejoice, joined to doing tov (H2896), good: the Preacher's counsel is never bare hedonism but gladness harnessed to goodness. This is the second 'nothing better' refrain (cf. 2:24).

13.text: And also this, that every man should eat and drink and see good in all his toil: this is the gift of God.
13.amp: And also that every man [adam] should eat [akal] and drink [shatah], and enjoy [raah — see] the good [tov] of all his labour [amal], it is the gift [mattath] of God [Elohim].
13.notes: mattath (H4991) is a grant, a thing bestowed: enjoyment is not wages earned but a present handed down. The same table that mocked the self-made king of chapter 2 feeds the man who receives it as gift.

14.text: I know that whatever God does stands forever; nothing can be added to it, and nothing taken from it. God has done it this way so that men would stand in awe before Him.
14.amp: I know [yada] that, whatsoever God [Elohim] does [asah], it shall be for ever [olam]: nothing [ayin] can be added [yasaph] to it, nor any thing taken [gara — diminished] from it: and God does it, that men should fear [yare — revere, stand in awe] before [panim] Him.
14.notes: yasaph (H3254) and gara (H1639), to add and to diminish: God's work needs no amendment and permits none. yare (H3372) is reverent awe, the fear that steadies rather than terrifies; permanence above is meant to produce worship below.

15.text: Whatever is has already been, and whatever will be has been already; and God seeks out again what has been driven into the past.
15.amp: That which has been is now [kebar — already]; and that which is to be has already been; and God [Elohim] requires [baqash — seeks out] that which is past [radaph — that which is driven away, pursued].
15.notes: kebar (H3528), 'already', twice: time's circle from chapter 1 restated, but with God now inside the sentence. baqash (H1245) with radaph (H7291), 'God seeks what is pursued away' (the KJV margin: 'that which is driven away'): nothing escapes into the past beyond His reach.

16.text: And I saw something more under the sun: in the place of justice, wickedness was sitting there, and in the place of righteousness, wickedness there too.
16.amp: And moreover I saw [raah] under the sun [shemesh] the place [maqom] of judgment [mishpat — justice], that wickedness [resha] was there; and the place of righteousness [tsedek], that iniquity [resha] was there.
16.notes: maqom (H4725), the place, twice: the courtroom itself, the one spot built for mishpat (H4941), occupied instead by resha (H7562), wickedness — the word repeated for both benches. The Preacher has moved from time's frustrations to justice's.

17.text: I said in my heart, 'God will judge the righteous and the wicked alike, for there is a time appointed there for every purpose and for every work.'
17.amp: I said [amar] in my heart [leb], God [Elohim] shall judge [shaphat] the righteous [tsaddiq] and the wicked [rasha]: for there is a time [et] there for every purpose [chephets] and for every work [maaseh].
17.notes: shaphat (H8199), to judge and set right: the answer to the corrupted courtroom is not despair but a better court. The poem's vocabulary returns — et (H6256), chephets (H2656) — because judgment too has its appointed hour, merely not yet.

18.text: I said in my heart concerning the state of the sons of man, 'God is sifting them, letting them see that in themselves, by themselves, they are beasts.'
18.amp: I said [amar] in my heart [leb] concerning the estate [dibrah — the matter, the case] of the sons of men [adam], that God [Elohim] might sift [barar — purge, test, make clear] them, and that they might see [raah] that they themselves are beasts [behemah].
18.notes: barar (H1305) is to sift and clarify, as grain is purged of chaff: mortality is God's sieve, shaking men down to what they are without Him. behemah (H929), beast: the comparison is diagnostic, not degrading — it measures man strictly under the sun.

19.text: For what befalls the sons of man befalls the beast; one and the same event awaits them both. As the one dies, so dies the other; they all draw one breath, and man has no advantage over the beast, for all is vapor.
19.amp: For that which befalls the sons of men [adam] befalls beasts [behemah]; even one [echad] thing befalls them: as the one dies [mavet], so dies the other; yea, they have all one breath [ruach]; so that a man has no preeminence [mothar — advantage, profit] above a beast: for all is vapor [hebel].
19.notes: ruach (H7307), breath: man and animal run on the same borrowed air. mothar (H4195) is kin to yithron, the profit-word — at the level of biology the ledger shows no human surplus, and mavet (H4194), death, collects from both accounts.

20.text: All go to one place: all came from the dust, and all return to the dust again.
20.amp: All go [halak] unto one [echad] place [maqom]; all are of the dust [afar], and all turn [shub] to dust again.
20.notes: afar (H6083) is the dust of Genesis 3:19, and shub (H7725), to return, is that verse's own verb: the Preacher is quoting the curse. One maqom (H4725), one destination, receives every walking thing.

21.text: Who really knows whether the spirit of the sons of man rises upward, and whether the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?
21.amp: Who knows [yada] the spirit [ruach] of man [adam] that goes up [alah — ascends], and the spirit of the beast [behemah] that goes down [yarad — descends] to the earth [eretz]?
21.notes: alah (H5927) and yarad (H3381), ascend and descend: the difference between man and beast is real but invisible from under the sun — who standing at a graveside can see which way a ruach (H7307) went? The book will answer at its close: the spirit returns to God who gave it (cf. Ecclesiastes 12:7).

22.text: So I saw that there is nothing better than for a man to rejoice in his own works, because that is his portion; for who can bring him back to see what will happen after him?
22.amp: Wherefore I perceive [raah] that there is nothing better [tov], than that a man [adam] should rejoice [samach] in his own works [maaseh]; for that is his portion [cheleq]: for who shall bring [bo] him to see what shall be after [achar] him?
22.notes: cheleq (H2506), the portion again: the present work, presently enjoyed, is the share a man can actually hold. achar (H310), what comes after, is sealed off from him — so the gift is today, and the refrain lands for the third time (cf. 2:24; 3:12).
